name: Alchi Kitchen
why_it_matters: Ladakh's first restaurant dedicated entirely to traditional Ladakhi cuisine. Founded by Nilza Wangmo, who took the Nari Shakti Puraskar (India's highest civilian honour for women) in 2019 for the work; an all-women kitchen in a chansa-style room a minute's walk from the monastery wall.
insider_tip: Wangmo runs a ₹1000 cooking class at 6pm where you make any three menu dishes — book the same morning. The chocolate momos sound gimmicky but are the after-monastery default for kids.
signature_address: Monastery Way, Alchi 194401, Leh District, Ladakh

name: Zimskhang Holiday Home Restaurant
why_it_matters: The dining room of a long-running family-run guest house run by Norboo Gailtsan, two minutes from the monastery. Its quiet garden setting across the lane from the rooms is what most day-trippers from Leh end up using when Alchi Kitchen has filled up.
insider_tip: Lunch is served buffet-style in season — useful when you're with a group. Skip the continental section and order off-menu thukpa fresh from the kitchen.

name: Alchi Resort Restaurant
signature_dish: Ladakhi vegetable thali with garden apricots
why_it_matters: Run on the heritage Alchi Lonpo land of the Toldan family, opened by Tsewang Toldan in 1998 and now managed by his son Tsewang Namgyal. The restaurant's apricot trees supply the kitchen — breakfast bowls are picked the same morning.
insider_tip: Mostly vegetarian — the kitchen flags the village's remoteness as the reason. Ask the day before if you want non-veg; they'll prep it fresh from Leh. Ideal for a packed-lunch order on the way to Lamayuru.
signature_address: Tukcha Yogma, Alchi 194401, Leh District, Ladakh

name: Legacy Hotel Alchi Restaurant
why_it_matters: The dining room of the Smanla (Amchi) family's hotel — they've been working in traditional Tibetan medicine and Ladakhi hospitality at Alchi for nearly two decades. Sits in an apricot-tree garden a short walk from the monastery, with Indus and Alchi Dam views.
insider_tip: Breakfast is the meal to come for; it's where the kitchen lets the Ladakhi side show. Ask for the noon chai (butter tea) even if it's not on your tray — it's part of the Amchi family ritual.
